utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. The Chamber was delayed coming in as had it to give consideration to another matter. I'm sorry for the delay. There is no witness. Are counsel wanting to move anything before the witness comes in or raise any matter? Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We're grateful for the time that Your Honour is allocating us for this matter. The Defence would wish to make a number of submissions in relation to issues of disclosure. We'd wish to make the submissions in the same spirit that we did the last time around, and, again, we will underline that we do not wish this to be perceived as an attack on our colleagues of the Prosecution. We wish to underline, however that what we believe to be violations of disclosure obligations Your Honour are very serious indeed in this case. In the last three weeks, the Defence has received a large quantity of new disclosure. Many of those were received as a result of particular requests made by the Defence to receive particular document which he had reason to believe that the Prosecution might have in its possession. Other documents came to the Defence as a result of Your Honour's order of a few weeks ago. Your Honour, so that the Chamber is aware of the type and scope of the problem in relation to this matter, I would like to give a sample of the material which the Prosecution has disclosed to the Defence in the past three weeks. One category of documents consist of, I believe, eight new investigator's notes taken by Mr. Howard Tucker. I would wish to point out that the notes were disclosed to the Defence after the witness had finished his testimony. A second category of disclosure, Your Honour, is an investigator note of a person called Mr. Colakovic. The reason we mention this note in particular, Your Honour, is that the Defence had sought to obtain any record of interview which related to this person and a number of other persons. And, for a year or so, the Prosecution told the Defence that no such note existed. This note, Your Honour, was taken in the presence of current investigator, Mr. Thomas Kuehnel. Another note, Your Honour, which has been recently disclosed to the Defence is a further investigator's notes taken from former Prosecution witness, Mr. Isni Ali, and, again, the document was disclosed after the termination of this witness's evidence. In addition, Your Honour - and I wish to be fair on that point - the document itself is not particularly relevant and would not have been particularly relevant to the evidence, we believe, and the cross-examination of this witness. A concern, however, is that three documents were apparently given by the witness to the Prosecution in the course of this interview, and those documents have apparently gone missing. Another matter, Your Honour, which -- or another document which had gone missing for a long time is an investigator note or the record of interviews of a person, whose name at this stage I would prefer not to mention, but who was a former security person of the president of the Republic of Macedonia, Mr. Trajkovski. As with the note of Mr. Colakovic, Defence had specifically requested to be provided with a record of any interviews or contact with that person for more than a year, we believe; and during that period, the Prosecution gave us the indication that no such record existed. The Defence persisted, however, with its request; and in the past three weeks, I believe, the Prosecution finally indicated to the Defence that there had indeed been such a meeting and a interview, but that the records of this meeting and interview have been lost. The matter is particularly serious, Your Honour, we submit, in relation to this witness, who we believe could have given important evidence in relation to the issue of control of the operation. In particular, the Prosecution was unable to indicate to the Defence which documents, if any, had been shown to this particular person. This person also, Your Honour, we indicate for the record was interviewed again by Mr. Kuehnel. Another note or statement that has gone missing is that of a journalist of the BBC, we believe, or the guardian, Mr. Nicholas Wood, who from other statements, Your Honour, and other pieces of evidence appears to have visited the village of Ljuboten on the 14th of August of 2001. The Defence in this case has been denied the benefit of that evidence since the statement appears to have gone missing. We believe that the statement of that witness, in view of the fact that he visited the village on the 14th, could have been relevant to at least three Prosecution witnesses and possibly many more. The Defence was also provided an additional two investigator's notes, again taken by Mr. Kuehnel, of Mr. Hutsch, a former Prosecution witness. Those, again, were received at the specific request and insistence of the Defence. I wish to indicate, however, that those additional two investigator's notes received, relating to Mr. Hutsch, were received in the middle of cross-examination so that the Defence was, in fact, in a position to use them. Your Honour, another document which the Defence received in the course of the last few weeks is a statement from a person called Mr. Camlovski, Viktor, who in his statement gives a indication, inter alia, that Judge Pancevski, an investigative judge which Your Honour would remember from having mentioned a number of time, was in fact investigating the allegation of mistreatment the detainees at the time. This, again, Your Honour, we believe is evidence that could and possibly should have been put through a number of Prosecution witnesses, in particular, Mr. Tucker or Dr. Jakovski. Another category of material and documents which the Defence has received in the course of the last weeks concerns a number of documents and investigator's notes that pertain to allegations of serious crimes committed in and around the area of Matejce, Your Honour. Your Honour will recall that Matejce is the area which was within the so-called zone of responsibility of the 114th Brigade of the NLA, the zone of responsibility of Mr. Bushi. That material, Your Honour, was received, again, after the departure of that witness. In the course of the last week, Your Honour, we have also received an additional note which has been prepared and taken from the note itself apparently by Mr. Bezruchenko himself from a former member of the army of the Republic of Macedonia. That note records, inter alia, the -- according to that person in any case, the presence of NLA in the village of Ljuboten. This note was taken in the year 2004 and had not been received by the Defence. Your Honour will also remember that, in his evidence, Mr. Bezruchenko indicated that he did not take personally interview, but that he would do so through the investigator. The note suggests that he alone was doing this interview. In the course of the past few days, the Defence has received a further set of disclosure in the form of a letter of the Prosecution which contained excerpts from documents, unidentified documents, which appear to be communications to and from the Prosecution, or records in any case, of meetings between representatives of the Prosecution and representatives of the local Macedonian judiciary. This document, Your Honour, is, again, relevant to the issue of the competence, to investigate the events of Ljuboten. In particular, there is a reference of a meeting between a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor and Judge Nikolovski, who was in charge of the investigation, who insisted at that time that certain material and certain result should be sent back to the local judicial authorities whom he says are competent to investigate these events. An additional set of material, Your Honour, is made of a miscellaneous group of statement and investigator's notes prepared or received by Mr. Kuehnel. Again, Your Honour, those were received at the insistence of the Defence on the basis that it should have in its possession all material prepared by this particular person who appears on the list of Prosecution witnesses. A last group of documents, Your Honour, pertain to the proposed future witness, Mr. -- not knowing whether he is protected or not, Your Honour, he is an NLA commander who is due to appear in this case. Your Honour, this is, in essence, the -- if not the extent, at least a good summary of the material which we have received in the past few weeks. The Defence submits that the prejudice which is suffered in this case is self-evident. This material, Your Honour, should have been disclosed in many case many years ago and in any case many months ago. The failure of the Prosecutor to disclose those documents to the Defence has prevented the Defence to investigate a number of these matter, if it had considered it to be necessary. It has also denied the Defence a opportunity, where appropriate and necessary, to test some of that material through cross-examination where relevant an appropriate. The Defence has also had to spend a great amount of time, Your Honour, in the past few weeks reviewing this material and establishing whether any of it could still be used through existing or forthcoming witnesses. We submit, Your Honour, that the Chamber itself could suffer as a result of this failure, to the extent that you would be denied potentially relevant material in these proceedings. Your Honour, we believe that the disclosure system relies heavily on the due diligence of the Prosecution, and Your Honours have made that point quite clearly in the past. The Defence should not be required, nor expected, to chase the Prosecution to ensure that material that is relevant to these proceedings is in fact disclosed. Your Honour, we believe that if the Chamber were minded to grant a remedy in this matter, this should be a stringent one that would be commensurate with what we say is a serious violations of the Prosecution's disclosure obligation. It should be one that would be capable of repairing or compensating the prejudice caused to the Defence. We submit, Your Honour, that the recalling of witnesses at this stage would not be an appropriate mechanism. It would only prolong the trial unnecessarily and in effect punish the defendants. The Defence will make a number of submissions as far as remedies are concerned, which the Chamber may find of assistance. Concerning the material which pertains to the forthcoming NLA commander, first, the Defence would wish to indicate that at this stage it reserves its right to ask that the commencement of the cross-examination of this witness be postponed or delayed should the Defence need more time to review this material. Considering also that the breach of those duties directly involves in many respect, and in large part, the fault of the investigator in this case, Mr. Kuehnel, the Defence submits that the Prosecution should not be permitted to call this person as a witness in this case. Concerning the material which pertains to crimes committed in the Matejce region, mostly in the form of investigator's notes taken by the Office of the Prosecutor, the Defence submits that the Chamber could take this failure into account when assessing the weight of the evidence, if any, to be given to the evidence of Mr. Bushi. Concerning, Your Honour, the material that pertains more specifically to Mr. Tucker, in particular the various notes and records that were provided recently to the Defence, we believe that one solution, or one matter which we will pursue and which at this stage doesn't require the intervention of the Chamber, would be for the Defence to submit a number of agreed facts based on the content of several of those notes, which we will submit to the Prosecution for their agreement. Should the Prosecution refuse or decline to agree with certain of these facts proposed fact, the Defence would come back to the Chamber, if necessary. Finally, Your Honour, concerning the material which has been misplaces or lost, at this stage the Defence would prefer to reserve its rights, consider whether there is any alternative course for the Defence to repair this matter, and perhaps, if necessary, come back to the Chamber for further submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I completely support the submission of my colleague Mr. Mettraux. In the interests of time, I wouldn't like to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, one bit of disclosure that my colleagues neglected to inform the Trial Chamber about was that last week the Prosecution disclosed some important exculpatory material related to the structure of the NLA which had been released by a Rule 70 provider a week ago Monday; and the same day that permission was provided to the Prosecution, this material was provided to the Defence. The Prosecution's request to -- to the provider for permission to disclose this material was made last April, but it was not until Monday that the provider finally provided some clearance to the Prosecution. Your Honour, most of the material that my colleague has mentioned the Prosecution has described in its submissions of 15 October 2007, the Prosecution's submissions pursuant to Rule 67 (C) concerning its review of material in its possession. And the Prosecution provided thesis submissions as it was coming to a close for the review, which it performed pursuant to Trial Chamber's order, I believe, of the 24th of September. I'm not specifically sure about that. Your Honour, my colleague mentioned a particular missing record of interview with a journalist, Mr. Nicholas Wood, and that missing record is noted in the Prosecution's written submissions. The Prosecution has been investigating what happened at that meeting and where any such records might be, and that task was been complicated by the fact by the person who led that meeting now lives and works in Cambodia; however, last week, contact was made with that person and that person indicated that that meeting with the journalist, Mr. Wood, was apparently an introductory meeting, a get-to-know-you meeting, to see if there would be any basis for further contact. Therefore, according to the person in Cambodia, that is why there is no record of interview or notes of a meeting or a statement; however, that person who is now working in Cambodia asked for a few more days in order for time to check his records, to make sure that his memory is correct. Your Honour, with respect to the claims by my learned colleagues that they are prejudiced by the recent disclosures of Prosecution, the Prosecution does not accept the fact that there is self-evident prejudice caused to the Defence. We are now still in the Prosecution's case in chief. There is time for the Defence to investigate information contained in these materials. Their case has not yet begun and will not begin for sometime yet. With respect to the Defence's ability to test this information or material through cross-examination, the Chamber already informed the Defence back in September that if the Defence felt it needed to do additional cross-examination on this material, it could make an application to recall one or more witnesses. Defence has not done that, but I assume that remedy to the Defence is still available. With respect to investigator notes recently disclosed that have been drafted by Mr. Howard Tucker - and these were notes that were found and disclosed after Mr. Tucker finished his testimony - these notes were not located previously because they had been saved on the personal drive of a former employee of the Prosecution, and that's why they had not been found before. We found these notes after we -- we did a search that we had been directed to do by the Trial Chamber. With respect to these investigator's notes by Mr. Howard Tucker, the Prosecution has repeatedly told the Defence that it would be willing to either recall Mr. Tucker and/or admit these investigator's notes, as they are as exhibits, as Defence exhibits, or both, if necessary. With respect to the request to delay the cross-examination of the witness who follows Mr. Bezruchenko, the Prosecution submits any further delay would be unwarranted and certainly would not be warranted based on the Prosecution's recent disclosures. These recent disclosures, to the best of my knowledge - I could be wrong - I don't believe they refer to the next witness, who is Mr. Ostreni, and the Defence certainly has time to review this material and use it during their cross-examination as they see fit. Indeed, the testimony of Mr. Ostreni has already been delayed repeatedly to give the Defence time to pursue further material that they might use for cross-examination. Your Honour, the suggestion, that these lapses in the Prosecution's disclosure work are largely due to mistakes by Mr. Kuehnel, is simply unfair. Has Mr. Kuehnel made some mistakes? Yes, he has and the Prosecution has acknowledged those mistakes. However, Your Honour, as the Appeals Chamber has noted, compliance with our disclosure obligations, obviously, it is important and we do take that seriously, but it is also, at times, a difficult burden. I have made mistakes, as you know, with respect to disclosure of relevant material, and there are simply sometimes mistakes that are made due to technical lapses or because of the lapse of time or the change over of personnel. But to cast a large part of the blame on one of the Prosecution's witnesses, and a very professional investigator, is simply not fair and not correct. With respect to the suggestion of submitting agreed facts vis-a-vis the investigator 8th's notes of Mr. Tucker, again, in the Prosecution's submission, it would make much more sense either to recall Mr. Tucker and have him cross-examined on these investigator's notes or to simply admit the investigator's notes themselves, and the Trial Chamber may determine whatever legal or factual conclusions it desires based on the content of this material. That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anything further, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will reflect upon the matters that have been raised. In the meantime, we should continue with other issues. Is there any other matter before the witness is brought back in; if not, we'll have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're sorry that other matters have delays us until now. May I remind you of the affirmation that you made which still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And now your questioning continues. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you very much Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Before we move forward, we'll move backwards a little bit to an issue that we discussed together last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown what is Exhibit P232, please. It's under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Bezruchenko, that I asked you last week whether you had seen that particular document in the course of your investigation, and you responded that you believed that -- or you did not think so. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It is page 6692, 6693, and also 6697, 6698 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid what I actually said, Mr. Mettraux, was that I saw a number of similar documents, but not necessarily this one. But having said that, well, it does not necessarily mean that this is not the document which I have not seen. Probably I have seen it; probably I have not. I just said that I had seen lots of documents of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, then, at page 6698 of the transcript that was on the 23rd of October of 2007, I asked you this: "Are you aware, Mr. Bezruchenko, whether your office and your colleagues made any efforts to verify whether the individuals which are mentioned by names in this particular document, as having received weapons in the Cair police station on the 11th of August, had in fact become de jure members of the MOI? Are you aware of that?" And your answer was "No." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then there was an exchange between Mr. Saxon and myself about the relevance of this. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that, sir. And if I may add at this point, I said that the document was dated 11 August 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I think that the relevant section of my report which deals with the events of Ljuboten, well, actually covers three days --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But do you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko --

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- not including August 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko, that what you told the Chamber about your absence of knowledge of the verifications being made in relation to the people mentioned on this document was not true. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. As I said, I probably have seen this document or maybe not. I'm not sure. But to give you a definitive answer, "yes" or "no" would be difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Bezruchenko. I have gone one step further from you seeing the document. When I asked whether you knew of the verifications that were being carried out by your office and whether you were aware of those efforts being made, your answer was "no." What I'm telling you now, Mr. Bezruchenko, is that, in fact, you knew very well what efforts were being made to verify the names mentioned on this document. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that efforts were being made regarding certain names of suspects who might have taken a role in the events of Ljuboten. That's right. But whether this particular name was there or not, I simply cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, what you told the Chamber last week, Mr. Bezruchenko, was gravely wrong because you yourself took part in the verification. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you mean by "verification," sir. There were a number of interviews done, I guess, and some of the interviews may have involved this particular person; but as I say, I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And what the result of those verification, which you said you were not aware of last week, were in fact damaging to your case. Is that correct, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not make such assessments, and I don't think I was really qualified to make such assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I will ask the registry to go to page 6 of that document. That would be N000-5189-ET-006. I believe that -- thank you very much. That's the correct page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, can you see the name on top of that document a person called Ljupco Savov? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the receipt underneath reads -- regards or concerns that person. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall meeting that person, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall that you, in fact, met that person in the course of a formal interview to which you participated?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not entirely certain. The name is a little unusual; therefore, I think I remember it. But if I ever met this person, that must have been in the course of a interview, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the course of the interview to which you participated with Mr. Ljupco Savov was for the purpose of verifying whether that person had, in fact, become a de jure member of the MOI and whether he had been in the village of Ljuboten on the 10, 11, or 12th August of 2001. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this is specifically correct, Mr. Mettraux. My interpretation of this fact would be a little bit different. I would rather say that he was interviewed in a number of broad issues related to the events of Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall, Mr. Bezruchenko, now that your memory has been refreshed, that you were present during that interview. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown what is Rule 65 ter 1D857, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters kindly ask the witness and the counsel to pause between questions and answers. We really have difficulty in interpreting. We don't have time to pronounce, and there is overlapping sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, we're being asked to pause again between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, do you recognise this investigator's note as having or as being the investigator's notes of Mr. Savov Ljupco, and it was taken on the 21st ever April of 2004. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And among those present is yourself, Viktor Bezruchenko. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If the registry could scroll down a little bit in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'd like to focus on the section of the interview which says: "Purpose of Interview," and I will read it out to you: "The above person is on the list of civilians that received weapons, uniforms, and ammunition at Cair police station either as volunteers or regular army/police reservists in August 2001. "On that course, Savov might be one of the potential participants present in Ljubanci or Ljuboten village in the period from 10th of August, 2001, until 12th of August," it should be 2001. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And will you agree that was indeed the purpose of the interview. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if the registry can focus or enlarge somewhat the bottom of the page, please, at paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, I will read out to you what the record says on this matter. It says that: "After ten or 15 days in July 2001, I again came to Bit Pazar police station, together with, last name unknown, Ljupco. We were sent from Bit Pazar police station to Cair police station. The time was about 17, 18 p.m. There were about 15, 20 civilians already there waiting also for uniforms and weapons," and then he goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if we can turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: In the last part of paragraph 3, he said: "The policeman asked me if I have a criminal background. I gave the policeman negative answer because I have no criminal records in Macedonia. Paragraph 4, it reads like this: "The policeman was not checking if it is true or not what I have told him about my criminal background. I have got dark green uniform, not camouflage, with a patch on one shoulder. I think it was combination of green and yellow colours written police. The shape of the patch, I think, looked like a triangle." Just stopping there for a second, Mr. Bezruchenko. Do you agree that the patch that Mr. Savov is describing here is the same as the patch or the picture of the patches that you showed -- that your office showed to a number of witnesses in this particular case? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It would appear so for from the description.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, this would be Exhibit P35 and P15, 1-5. Then, if you could turn to paragraph 6, if the registry could scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Savov told you this: "After receiving uniforms and weapons, the policeman asked both of us to give him our phone numbers just to let us know whether it will be something. I did not receive any identification card of reserve police officer from the Ministry of Interior." Then: "I left the police station with weapon, ammunition and uniform, and I came back home." Then at paragraph 8, it say this: "Sometimes at the end of August 2001, I think it was on 23rd or 25th of August, I have received a phone call and a man voice introducing as a policeman from Cair police station told me to bring back to the Cair police station uniform, weapon. And ammunition. I brought it there at the same day, and I signed the handing over document." Then, at paragraph 9, it says this: "I have never been activated as a volunteer reservist." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko, that contrary to what you told this Chamber last week, you in fact took a direct and personal part in the interview of the people who appeared on this document, with a view to ascertain whether they had become de jure members of MOI and whether they had been in the village of Ljuboten on the 10, 11, or 12th of August?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in fact I never said anything like this. What I said was that I was, indeed, involved in a number of interviews, with various people, including the suspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you what you also said, you will recall, Mr. Bezruchenko, is that you were not aware of any verification being made as to whether any of those people had become de jure members of the MOI. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recalling saying that I was involved in a number of interviews on a broad range of issues related to suspects of the events in Ljuboten. This is what I said, not necessarily giving individuals you are now ascribing to me, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree with the proposition, sir, that this particular as secretary of your work - and I will come back to other aspects - had nothing to do with military analysis? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, Mr. Bezruchenko, that this, your involvement in the interview of that person, falls within the definition of military analysis as given by you to the Office of the Prosecutor in your evidence in chief?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters would like to ask the witness and counsel not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... issues related to military matters. Obviously, their statements speaks of such things as weapons, uniforms, ammunition. So I don't really see any reason for not being -- I mean, I really don't see any reason for not being involved in analysis of these kind of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the witness please what is shown Rule 65 ter 1D554.1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And before it appears, Mr. Bezruchenko, is that correct that you and your office -- well, let me ask you this: Are you aware of the that your office sought to verify whether a number of other individuals, not just Mr. Savov, but a number of other individuals had in fact become de jure members of the MOI and whether they had been in the village of Ljuboten at the relevant time? I'm talking of people who appear on this or other similar lists.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that the investigation was going on and was focussing, obviously, on various possible suspects, probably including these people as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, before we go further, let me show you this particular document, Mr. Bezruchenko. This is a letter from the Defence sent to the Macedonian authorities; and on this particular document, the Defence sought to obtain information whether any of the persons in this document had -- including Mr. Savov Ljupco, as you can see at number 4, whether any of those people had received a salary from the MOI during the period 1st August through 30 September of 2001. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the document with subject, "Request for data"?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can you see that the specific requests made by the Defence concerns eight individuals who are the same eight individuals who are mentioned on the previous documents that you showed you. Do you recognise those names, including Mr. Savov?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this name is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recognise the other names that are on this list?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think two or three, perhaps, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree that those names are the same names as those which appeared on the previous document that I showed you, that is.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would appear so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree that the request made by the Defence was to the effect that it wished to receive information whether these eight people received salary from the MOI during the period 1st August, 2001, to 30th September, 2001. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would appear so, sir, but this is the first time I actually ever see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let me show you another document then.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's Rule 65 ter 1D554.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: As you can see, Mr. Bezruchenko, this is a letter written by the Cabinet of the State Secretary within the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Macedonia. It is dated the 5th of June of 2007, and this is sent to a colleague from the Defence team of Mr. Boskoski. It is, in fact, a response to the previous letter that I have shown you, and I'd like to read to you the content of that letter. It says this: "With respect to your request on whether the listed persons in your request have received salary from the MOI, during the period of 1st August 2001 to 30 September 2001, we inform you that those persons are not listed on the salary lists of the Ministry; and, until this day, they have not received salary in the MOI in any period." It is signed by the State Secretary, Mr. Djuclevski [phoen]. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, in fact, Mr. Bezruchenko, you will agree that this information, perhaps not to the complete extent that it would apply to the eight persons, but the fact that many of the people listed in this document and other similar documents had never become de jure member of the MOI, you were aware of that fact. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. Let me put it this way: This is the first time I see this document. I don't really think I saw it before. And, secondly, as I say, my focus as a military analyst was not really focussed on this particular issue. There were other issues that were in the focus of my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But, Mr. Bezruchenko, you have just indicated to the Trial Chamber that the interview of Mr. Savov failed, you say, straight within the compass of your duties as a military analyst. Are you saying that, in fact, this issue falls beyond the realm of your competence of a military analyst?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that. What I'm saying is there is was many issues that I was dealing with, primarily issues related to the conflict, as well as weapons, ammunition, and other matters, but I don't remember seeing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But let me ask my question again, Mr. Bezruchenko, and forget this particular document for a moment. Is that correct that result or as part of your work for the Office of the Prosecutor, you became aware of similar information; namely, to the effect that a number of individuals who appeared on this particular list of receipts, which I have shown you, and other similar lists had never become de jure members of the MOI? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in those specific terms that you describe.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bezruchenko, let's be quite clear about that. Is that correct that you personally took part in a number of interviews which related to that particular issue? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in a number of interviews which related to the events which took place in Ljuboten in August 2001?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko, that you took part, in particular, in the interview of a number of people who are listed on this document I have shown you, as well as other similar documents where their name appear? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that I was involved in a number of interviews. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'd like you to answer the question, Mr. Bezruchenko, more specifically in relation to people whose name mentioned on the document that I have shown you and other similar documents. Do you agree you did attend such interviews?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned, I was involved in a number of interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Including of people whose name appear on the lists that I have shown you and other similar listings. Do you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And as part of those interview, Mr. Bezruchenko, you became aware of the fact that a number of them had, in fact, never become de jure members of the MOI. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would appear that some of them said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And a number of them, following those interviews, you also became aware of the fact that they had not been in the village of Ljuboten during the relevant weekend. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would appear that some of them said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown what is exhibit P31 -- I'm sorry P231. It's under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, do you have that list in front of you on your screen?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recognise that list?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I have seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bezruchenko, do you agree that, or is it within your knowledge perhaps, that this document was prepared by a person known by the pseudonym M-053.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned previously, Mr. Mettraux, with all my due respect, I don't think I actually saw this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let's look at its content then, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If the --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Would you look through the list of names that appear on the first page and indicate whether you know any of the persons who appear on that first page.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not certain, but I think I remember somebody by name Milosevski, which is number 8 on the list. This would be the person. Well, the others, I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Isn't that correct, Mr. Bezruchenko, that you also know the person under number 9.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps, probably, if he was interviewed in the course of a interview at which I was present, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the registry please turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recognise any name that is familiar to you on this page, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really. I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the registry please turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recognise any name that is familiar to you on this page, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think number 20 and number 21, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And those, again, would be persons that you interviewed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the registry please turn to the next page. Your Honour, I mentioned M-053. My precious assistant indicated it is, in fact, M-084.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will ask you the same question, Mr. Bezruchenko. Do you recognise any name on that particular page.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the third name from -- sorry, the second name from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that would Mr. Milosevski Samdaj [phoen]. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that is, again, someone whom you interviewed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would appear to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the registry please turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recognise any name of persons whom you know on this particular page, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure, but I think possibly could be the second and third names.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So Mr. Vanco Conjkovski and Mr. Boris Kostencovksi. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I could only definitely say it after I saw my notes or the notes of the investigator who was doing this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, while we're here, let me ask you this: Did you keep any notes of these interviews which you conducted or took part in?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the registry please turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you know of any person whose name would be familiar to you on that page?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Maybe the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That would be Ljupco Stojanovski. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the registry please turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you know the person whose named on this page, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the registry please turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you know the name of either of these people?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'll ask you the question already, but I'll ask you specifically about one particular witness who you have interviewed. Do you recall interviewing or taking part in the interview of Mr. Sladinovski Zoran, whose name appear on this list?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name seems to be familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall that he was asked questions about his whereabouts in -- during the relevant period of 10 to 12 August and also about the receipt of a rifle or semi-automatic rifle and rounds of ammunition. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you mentioned, the name seems to be familiar, but I cannot really be certain. But he probably was asked these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that would be the same for the others. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown what is Rule 65 ter 1D939, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Before I ask you to look into the document, Mr. Bezruchenko, do you recall how many people on that list of 40 were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor? Is the number known to you?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you know, of all those whom you've interviewed, how many turned out to be not members of the MOI? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the document which you have in front of you. This is a statement taken by the Defence team of Mr. Boskoski, and it is a statement of Mr. Popovski Gjoko. And as you can see from paragraph 2, Mr. Gjoko work in the Ministry of Interior in the sector for financial, material, technical, and logical matters with the deputy assistant minister. And, paragraph 3, Mr. Gjoko indicates that: "From the Defence, I was given a list of 40 persons, stipulated in the request of information submitted to the MOI."

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And simply for the record, the list itself is the third page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And he say this is: "I was asked to check whether the listed persons, from August 1st, 2001 until September 30, 2001 year, were members of the regular or reserve structure of the police and whether they received salaries in the mentioned periods from MOI." And he says: "I am signing and submitting the list as appendix to this statement." Then at paragraph 5, he say this is: "I made insight in the MOI's archive and in the sector for finances in MOI. After the conducted check in the records of deployed members of the reserve structure of the police for the above mentioned period, I concluded that larger part of the persons whose names are stipulated in the statement were not members of the deployed reserve police members, and they not recorded on the salary list in MOI. And, so far, they have not received payment from MOI in any period." And then he goes on to add this: "After the conducted check, I have established that eight of the mentioned persons were engaged in MOI as members of the reserve structure and received salaries for the period from August 1st, 2001 until September 20th, 2001, as follows," and there is at list of knows names. And then in paragraph 7, he says: For two persons from mentioned list - and that is for Kostencovski Bozin Zoran and Ovcazski Mirko Kirco - I could not find at all information in the registration record. If I could have at disposal the unique personal identification numbers from these persons, I could give information for them as well." Do you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko, that on the basis of this statement, and on the basis at least of the verifications that were made by this person within the archive and records of the Ministry of Interior, only eight of the 40 persons who appeared on the document that I have shown to you a moment ago in fact became de jure member of the MOI? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say, Mr. Mettraux, this is the first time I actually see this document, and it probably require little bit longer for me to actually ascertain the significance and value of this document. So just to answer this question you directly "yes" or "no" flatly, I simply am not in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, at this stage, Mr. Bezruchenko, I will just ask you to confirm whether that is what the document suggests. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears that the document suggests an investigation into this matter was apparently made, and, apparently, some names have been identified as belonging to the people who were in -- on the payroll on Ministry of Interior, between August 1st and September 20th, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree that these people account for eight of the 40 which with mentioned on the list that I showed you before? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that a more proper investigation should be made in each particular case. There would be name sakes. It could be the case of wrong identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But simply to move on, Mr. Beruchenko, do you agree at least that's what the document says?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am afraid I cannot offer all my comments on this point, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this then: Do you agree as part of your own investigation, and you have indicated already, You, the Office of the Prosecutor, in your own investigation had already realised or come to the realisation that a number of these individuals, including Mr. Savov, had not become de jure member of the police? Do you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mettraux, as I mentioned previously, this is the first time I see this document, and this document is dated September 2007. I don't think that in September 2007 I was really working on identification of anyone who was involved in the events of Ljuboten because my report was practically done at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Bezruchenko. I'll move on to ask you a few more questions about what you say your position and role in the Office of the Prosecutor has been since you were first employed, and I will ask you this first: Do you recall being asked by Mr. Saxon to define your role and duty as a military analyst on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, do you remember, on the 4th of October?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you described it in the following terms to the Chamber, and That's at page 6055: "Essentially, this position entails providing military dimension to organisations, individuals, and events related to a armed conflict or a war." Then, you added the following: "Well, essentially that means that military -- I'm doing military analysis which covers or may cover such areas as structure and armament of the armies or warring parties involved in the conflict. They are organisations, factions, command and control issues, strategy, tactics, operations on the ground, and such functional issues as operations, logistics, security, finance, training, and so on." And that's still the 4th of October, 2007, page 6055. Do you recall giving that description?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this description, and I also remember that actually you suggested that I should stop reading from the -- from my folder and you just cut me short.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct that, in terms of responsibilities and duties, Mr. Bezruchenko, the role of military analyst, such as you are, and the role of an investigator would be different? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you agree that an investigator with the Office of the Prosecutor would, for instance, look for documents and evidence that could be relevant to the charges that it would interview or take part in interviews of witnesses, and that he would be in touch with the local authorities as might be relevant to the investigation? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor would also be the one competent to send requests for assistance or requests for material on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And it's also the role of the investigator to seize material where necessary and appropriate on behalf of the office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And it's also the role of the investigator to review material obtained as a result of investigation or requests for information. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you also agree that one of the practical differences between an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor and a military analyst, by reason of their different role, is that an investigator cannot be called as an expert witness, but that sometimes a military analyst can. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I can entirely agree with that because I know of instances when investigators were also called in the role of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Bezruchenko. But you agree that never has an investigator been called as a expert on behalf of the Prosecutor, or do you know of any such incidents?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko, that, in fact, you were always much more to the investigation team of the Office of the Prosecutor than a military analyst. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was performing my functions as military analyst to the best of my knowledge and to the best of my job description.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, I would not wish the question asked here to be perceived as a criticism of the way in which you conducted your duties, but do you agree that you did much more for that investigation than just being a military analyst as you described to Mr. Saxon? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please qualify your question, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko, that you took a full part in the investigation and preparation of this case for trial?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved in a number of interviews, and they was asking my opinion on a number of issues. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let's take it one step at a time then. Do you agree that you took part, as you just indicated, in the interviews of many potential Prosecution witnesses in the course of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved in a number of interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Are you able, Mr. Bezruchenko, to state, approximately, how many interviews you believe you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not too many; perhaps about a dozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, would about 30 be more accurate, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 30? Well, maybe about 20, but 30 would be a little bit of an exaggeration, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, would 25, then, be about right?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply cannot tell, because it really requires an exact counting; but, approximately, about 20 I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall interviewing Mr. Isovski Saso.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present at this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall Mr. Cvetenovski Zoran?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you were present during his interview?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And so with Mr. Nikolovski Kiro?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the other persons who you have indicated on the list of 40 persons that we've gone through. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct that some of those people whom you've interviewed, or the interview of which you've attended, have later become Prosecution witnesses?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it also correct that during those interviews, you personally asked many questions of the witnesses? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the questions were directed through the investigator and under his supervision.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Bezruchenko, that the questions that you asked were put directly to the witness and directly answered by the witness, too. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned, Mr. Mettraux, the questions were directed to the witness since he was the person interviewed, but they directed through the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And when you suggest that they were directed through the investigator, Mr. Bezruchenko, what do you suggest exactly?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that during the interview, the investigator would actually ask the questions which were discussing with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, Mr. Bezruchenko, that your questions were then asked on your behalf by the investigator?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, when we break, we were discussing the questioning by you of witnesses, and the indication that you gave that you would do that through the investigator. That's page 37, line 3 to 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the registry please bring up what is Rule 65 ter 1D936, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, are you familiar with this record? This is a record of a interview conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor with Mr. Sokol Mitrovski, and it's dated the 1st of August, 2004?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the registry please turn to page 26 of that document. That would be 1D00-794, and if the registry to focus on the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If you could look at the last three line of that page first, Mr. Bezruchenko, it is in the course of the interview. It has already been 45 pages or so, and then are you recorded as saying this: "Can I ask a question?" And the investigator, Mr. Kuehnel, says: "Please, please. Go ahead." And then yourself, you say: "I have about ten questions."

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if the registry could turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, there, Mr. Bezruchenko, as you can see, you are asking a number of questions of Mr. Mitrovski. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree that those questions are asked directly by you and answered directly to you by Mr. Mitrovski. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way it worked usually as follows: Normally, my questions would refer to various matters which really needed to be specified or qualified, because the investigator would normally have a limited knowledge of certain military matters, and I always asked his permission to ask a question or not. If he believed that this was question was relevant for the investigation, and his line of questioning in fact, he would actually agree with me. If he believed it was not the case, then he would disagree with me. So, basically, it was all done in line with his decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you the question, again: Do you agree that the questions asked by you directly to the witness and that the witness answers directly to you. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you go also that Mr. Kuehnel is not being asked at every turn of the way for every one of your question, whether he agrees or not with your question, the flow is just going between you and Mr. Mitrovksi? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was going on among the three of us, since we are all three were equally involved.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters kindly ask you, once again, to pause between question and answer. It is very important for our work and the work the transcript to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters. Can the registry scroll down a bit to the bottom of page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you agree that on that page, Mr. Bezruchenko, there is no involvement whatsoever of Mr. Kuehnel?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it I would appear so, perhaps because it was a discussion of strictly specific military matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the registry please turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, there, do you agree that your questioning of Mr. Mitrovski just goes on and, again, no involvement of Mr. Kuehnel. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The registry can scroll down the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the registry please turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree that, again, your questioning of Mr. Mitrovski just goes on, and there's still no involvement and no questioning or intervention of Mr. Kuehnel? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is something which should be regarded perhaps in a somewhat broader context. As you probably noted, Mr. Mettraux, my questions came at the very end of the interview, and they were limited to strictly military matters. In fact, most part of the interview was taken up by the questions of the investigator. I had only about ten questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, that's not quite right, Mr. Bezruchenko. This line of questioning is to be found at page 46 -- this particular line of questioning between page 46 and 57 of a record of interview that is 111 pages long, so you're right in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But I will ask the registry to turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do agree that your questioning and interviewing of Mr. Mitrovski, again, just goes on questions and after questions without the involvement or the intervention of Mr. Kuehnel.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really think can I comment on that anymore. As I said, I was involved in the interview; and whenever the subject was related to any particular military matter, well, I asked Mr. Kuehnel's permission and I could ask my own questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But do you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko, that you were not a single a time, apart from the first question, asking for the permission of Mr. Kuehnel. The interview between you and Mr. Mitrovski goes on without any involvement of Mr. Kuehnel at this stage? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that. Mr. Kuehnel was involved in the entirety of this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the registry please turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you agree that, again, the questioning just goes on between you and Mitrovski for mother page, and there is no involvement of Mr. Kuehnel? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say this: This record of interview which is going on. On this particular page now, there is probably not the involvement of Mr. Kuehnel. So what?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, again, if you can look at this particular page of that transcript, do you agree that the interview between you and Mr. Mitrovski just goes on, and no involvement of Mr. Kuehnel? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a interview between me and Mr. Mitrovski. It was an interview between Mr. Mitrovski, Mr. Kuehnel, and with Mr. Bezruchenko involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can we please turn to the next page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko, that, again, on this page, the questions only come from you and the answers from the witness Mitrovski, and that will there is, again, no involvement and no question put by Mr. Kuehnel? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this is the question which is really appropriate me to answer, Mr. Mettraux. You can probably ask this question of Mr. Kuehnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, at this stage, I will ask you, Mr. Bezruchenko, to answer this question. Is that correct that on this particular page of the record of interview - that's page 53 - there's a list of questions asked by you and a list of answer from Mr. Mitrovski, and no involvement of Mr. Kuehnel. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this particular page, yes, that would appear so?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if the registry can turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you look at the top of that page first, can you see that Mr. Kuehnel is now asking his first question in seven or eight pages. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see his comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can you see that the rest of the page continues with questions asked by you and answered directly from the witness. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you agree that still goes on the next page of the transcript. This is you requesting questions, the witness answering, and no involvement of Mr. Kuehnel? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, again, as with the previous ten or so pages, this is you asking question of the witness and him answering to you, without involvement of Mr. Kuehnel. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this would appear so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if we can to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you agree that still is the case, until the point where you suggest to take a break. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, sometimes it would really take a long time to get the appropriate answer to a question. So whenever there was an exchange going on, well, it would probably cover a few pages, maybe even a few dozen pages, to get the appropriate answer to a appropriate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But do you agree that what we've just seen, Mr. Bezruchenko, in fact, is you interviewing the witness? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. I was asking some specific questions in the course of the interview; and if there was a requirement to specify a question with another question, this is what I had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree that asking questions in the course of an interview would qualify as conducting a interview or interviewing? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. I don't think it would amount to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you agree that you were asked questions of Mr. Mitrovski in several other parts of the record of interview at a later stage in particular in the record? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some questions were asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you continued asking those questions all through the interview up to its very end. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since this was the interview about most military matters, and we were in fact in full agreement with the investigator -- with the investigator on this issue, some of the questions were suggested by me to asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, the questions were not just suggested by you. Is that correct, Mr. Bezruchenko. They were asked by you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that also correct that you asked questions of other witnesses whom were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. I don't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you agree that as you did with Mr. Mitrovski, which is to ask questions of him, you did the same thing with other witnesses that were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned previously, I was involved in the other interviews, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And as part of this involvement, you asked questions of witnesses. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, through the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And when you mean "through the investigator," you mean, again, that you asked the question directly with the investigator present. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that I always asked the investigator's permission to ask this or that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree that when that happened, you asked the question directly of the witness. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, normally, I would ask the investigator whether he would like to ask this or that question; and if he said, "Yes, you can go ahead," I just went ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But, in that particular instance which we've just gone through, Mr. Bezruchenko, do you agree that you did not do that. You did not ask Mr. Kuehnel whether you could ask that or that question. You just went ahead and asked them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because you cannot really make the conclusion on the face value of one record, Mr. Mettraux, because when there is a dialogue going on, there is much more than is remained on paper. There are gestures, there are suggestions, and there was a lively discussion. So if there was at any point a desire on the part of anyone to interrupt, that's what I was doing. That happens, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall asking questions of, among other people, Mr. Mitre Despodov?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Rule 65 ter 2D293, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document as the record of interview of Mr. Despodov Mitrevski, on the 31st of July, 2004?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall being present during that interview?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the registry please turn to page 24 of that document. It is 2D02-1691.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If you look at the top of the page, there is Mr. Kuehnel asking a question. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then there's Mr. Despodov answering. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
